\framekicker{Learning outcomes}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Session Objectives}
\leadpar{By the end of this session, participants can:}
\begin{isteps}
\item Choose the correct \textbf{output activation and loss function} for binary, multiclass, and regression tasks --- without guessing.
\item Prepare text with \textbf{multi-hot encoding}, and labels as either \textbf{one-hot} or \textbf{sparse integers}.
\item Read a \textbf{validation loss curve} to find the best stopping point, then retrain to exactly that point.
\item Recognise an \textbf{information bottleneck} and size intermediate layers from the number of classes.
\item Normalise features using \textbf{training-set statistics only}, and evaluate a small-data model with \textbf{K-fold cross-validation}.
\end{isteps}

\framekicker{Vocabulary}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Terms used precisely from here to chapter 20}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}

\thead{Term} & \thead{Meaning} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Sample / input} & One data point entering the model. \\
\textbf{Prediction / output} & What comes out. \\
\textbf{Target} & The ground truth, from outside the model. \\
\textbf{Loss value} & A measure of distance between the two. \\
\textbf{Mini-batch} & Typically 8--128 samples at a time. \\
\end{itable}

\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.376\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.564\textwidth}}
\thead{Task type} & \thead{Defining feature} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Binary classification} & Two mutually exclusive categories. \\
\textbf{Multiclass} & More than two, one label per sample. \\
\textbf{Multilabel} & A sample may carry several labels at once. \\
\textbf{Scalar regression} & One continuous value. \\
\textbf{Vector regression} & Several continuous values. \\
\end{itable}

\end{minipage}%

\framekicker{Vocabulary}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The distinction that decides your output layer}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch04-heads.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Multiclass and multilabel look similar and need different heads.\par}
\begin{iband}[signal]
\textbf{Softmax} forces the outputs to sum to 1 --- right when exactly one class is true. \textbf{Sigmoid per class} lets several be true at once. Choosing the wrong one \hilite{trains a model that cannot express the answer}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\coursesection{01}{Binary classification: IMDB reviews}{50,000 movie reviews, positive or negative.}

\framekicker{Section 4.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The dataset, and what has already been done to it}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}IMDB ships with Keras, already split and already converted from words into integer indices. \inlinecode{num\_words=10000} keeps only the ten thousand most frequent words.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 4.1 --- loading IMDB}{listings/ch04-01.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch04-02.txt}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The split is balanced 50:50, which matters for the baseline we set in a moment.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Turning a list of words into a tensor}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}A \inlinecode{Dense} layer needs a fixed-length numeric vector, but reviews have different lengths. Multi-hot encoding solves that by turning each review into a 10,000-long vector of 0s and 1s.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 4.2 --- multi-hot encoding}{listings/ch04-03.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch04-04.txt}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{What that encoding throws away}
\begin{iband}[amber]
Multi-hot records \textbf{which words appear}, not \textbf{in what order}. \textit{"good, not bad"} and \textit{"bad, not good"} become \hilite{the identical vector}
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}For sentiment on long reviews that turns out to be good enough. Chapters 14 and 15 replace it as soon as word order starts to carry the meaning.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{A deliberately small model}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Two 16-unit hidden layers and a single sigmoid output. The model is kept small on purpose --- the dataset is not large, and chapter 5 explains what happens when it is not.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 4.3 --- the model}{listings/ch04-05.py}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\inlinecode{relu} zeroes out negatives; \inlinecode{sigmoid} squashes the final score into the interval [0, 1] so it can be read as a probability.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Why crossentropy and not mean squared error}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{Crossentropy is a quantity from the field of information theory that measures the distance between probability distributions.}\quotecite{Chollet \& Watson, section 4.1}
\end{iquote}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The model outputs a \textbf{distribution}; the target is a distribution too. Crossentropy is the natural way to compare them, which is why it pairs with sigmoid and softmax rather than MSE.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Holding out a validation set, and training long}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Ten thousand samples are set aside. The model is then trained for \textbf{20 epochs --- deliberately too many} --- so the turning point becomes visible.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 4.4--4.5 --- validate and fit}{listings/ch04-06.py}
\begin{iband}[signal]
Training past the optimum is not waste here --- it is \hilite{how you find the optimum}. The next slide shows what the curves say.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{What the two curves do}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\begin{ibullets}
\item \textbf{Training loss} falls monotonically, epoch after epoch.
\item \textbf{Validation loss} falls, bottoms out around \textbf{epoch 4}, then \hilite{turns and climbs}.
\end{ibullets}

\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\begin{iband}[amber]
Everything after epoch 4 makes the model \textbf{better on data it has seen and worse on data it has not}.
\end{iband}

\end{minipage}%
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{After the fourth epoch, you're overoptimizing on the training data, and you end up learning representations that are specific to the training data and don't generalize to data outside of the training set.}\quotecite{Chollet \& Watson, section 4.1}
\end{iquote}
\end{frame}
\note{This pattern reappears in every later chapter. Train to see the turning point, then retrain to it.}

\framekicker{Section 4.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The procedure, stated once and reused everywhere}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch04-curve.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Overtraining is used as a measuring instrument, then discarded.\par}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Retrain to four epochs, and score it once}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}With the turning point known, build a fresh model and stop at exactly that epoch. Only now does the test set get touched.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{the production run}{listings/ch04-07.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch04-08.txt}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\istat{88\%}{test accuracy after retraining to 4 epochs}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\istat{50\%}{the random baseline --- the classes are balanced}
\end{minipage}%
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Reading a prediction back}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}A binary model returns one number per sample. Turning it into a decision means choosing a threshold --- and that choice belongs to the business, not to the model.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{predicting on new reviews}{listings/ch04-09.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch04-10.txt}
\begin{iband}[signal]
Note the third review at \textbf{0.67} --- confident enough to call positive at a 0.5 threshold, and negative at 0.7. Chapter 6 shows how to set that number \hilite{against a cost, not a habit}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\coursesection{02}{Multiclass: Reuters newswires}{46 topics, mutually exclusive.}

\framekicker{Section 4.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Same shape of problem, more classes}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}8,982 training and 2,246 test newswires, each belonging to exactly one of 46 topics. The inputs are encoded exactly as before; only the labels and the output layer change.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 4.9 --- loading Reuters}{listings/ch04-11.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch04-12.txt}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Two ways to write the labels}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The same information can be given to Keras in two shapes. The maths is identical; only the interface differs.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\icode{python}{one-hot labels}{listings/ch04-13.py}

\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\icode{python}{sparse integer labels}{listings/ch04-14.py}

\end{minipage}%
\begin{iband}[signal]
Pick whichever avoids a conversion. Mixing them up gives a shape error that names the loss function, \hilite{which is the clue to what went wrong}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The model, and a metric that asks a better question}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The hidden layers are wider than in the IMDB example --- the next slide explains why --- and a second metric is added.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 4.11 --- model and top-K}{listings/ch04-15.py}
\begin{iband}[signal]
\textbf{Top-K accuracy} asks whether the true class is among the top k guesses. For a system that \hilite{suggests rather than decides}, that is often the honest measure.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{An experiment designed to fail}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch04-bottleneck.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont The same network, except one intermediate layer is squeezed to four units.\par}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The book deliberately builds the broken version to show what an \textbf{information bottleneck} does. Squeezing 46 classes through 4 dimensions loses information \hilite{that no later layer can recover}\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{What the bottleneck costs}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}One line changes: the second hidden layer drops from 64 units to 4. Everything else about the network and the training run is identical.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 4.13 --- the broken model}{listings/ch04-16.py}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\istat{$\approx$ 80\%}{validation accuracy without the bottleneck}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\istat{$\approx$ 71\%}{with it --- nine points gone}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{The model is able to cram most of the necessary information into these 4-dimensional representations, but not all of it.}\quotecite{Chollet \& Watson, section 4.2}
\end{iquote}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The sizing rule that follows}
\begin{iband}[signal]
\textbf{An intermediate layer should not be narrower than the number of output classes.} That is why IMDB was fine on 16 units (2 classes) and Reuters needs 64.
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}It is a floor, not a target. Chapter 5 covers how to find the right size above that floor.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}
\note{The failed experiment is the best part of chapter 4. Show it in full --- people learn more from it than from the working version.}

\framekicker{Section 4.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Retrain, evaluate, and check against the right baseline}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Same procedure as IMDB: the curve turns at epoch 9, so a fresh model is trained to exactly nine epochs.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 4.14 --- production model}{listings/ch04-17.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch04-18.txt}
\begin{iband}[signal]
80\% sounds unremarkable until you know the baseline: guessing according to the class frequencies gets about \textbf{19\%}, because the 46 classes are \hilite{far from evenly distributed}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Where the remaining 20\% goes}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Roughly one newswire in five is misfiled. Looking at the confusion between classes tells you whether that matters.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{inspecting the errors}{listings/ch04-19.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch04-20.txt}
\begin{iband}[amber]
Class 3 alone accounts for \textbf{813 of 2,246} test samples. That imbalance is why the honest baseline is 19\% rather than 1/46 --- and why \hilite{accuracy alone is a thin way to describe this model}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\coursesection{03}{Scalar regression: house prices}{Very little data. The rules change.}

\framekicker{Section 4.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{480 training samples, eight features}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}A small extract of the 1990 California census: 480 training and 120 test districts, each described by eight numeric features, with median house price as the target.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 4.16 --- loading the data}{listings/ch04-21.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch04-22.txt}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Features: longitude, latitude, median house age, population, households, median income, total rooms, total bedrooms.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Normalisation --- and the leak hiding in it}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The features live on wildly different scales, which destabilises optimisation. Each is centred and scaled --- but look carefully at which statistics are used.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 4.17 --- normalising}{listings/ch04-23.py}
\begin{iband}[rose]
Recomputing \inlinecode{mean} and \inlinecode{std} from the test data would be an \hilite{information leak}: the model would know something about data it is supposed never to have seen. Chapter 5 gives this its formal name.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Which statistics may touch which data}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch04-leak.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont The rule in one picture: statistics flow outward from the training set only.\par}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{A regression head has no activation}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Three design choices here differ from the classifiers, and each follows from the task or the data size.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 4.18 --- the model}{listings/ch04-24.py}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icardaccent}
\cardh{No output activation}
A sigmoid would trap predictions in [0, 1]. Regression must be free.
\end{icardaccent}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icardwarn}
\cardh{A small model}
480 samples. A large model would simply memorise them.
\end{icardwarn}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icardaccent}
\cardh{MSE to train, MAE to read}
MAE is human-readable: 0.5 means being off by about \$50,000.
\end{icardaccent}
\end{minipage}%
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{With this little data, one validation split is not enough}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch04-kfold.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Each quarter takes a turn as the validation set; the four scores are averaged.\par}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}With 480 samples, a single split of, say, 120 is small enough that the score depends heavily on \hilite{which 120 you happen to draw}\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{K-fold, written out}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The loop below carves out fold \textit{i}, trains a \textbf{brand-new} model on the rest, and records its validation MAE.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 4.19 --- the K-fold loop}{listings/ch04-25.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch04-26.txt}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The spread is the point}
\begin{iband}[amber]
The four folds scored \textbf{0.232 to 0.349} --- a spread of nearly 50\% of the smallest value. Any single split would have reported one of those numbers and \hilite{told you nothing about the other three}
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}That variance is exactly why K-fold exists, and why it is worth four times the compute on a dataset this size.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{How long to train? Average the curves}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Run the folds again for 200 epochs, keep the per-epoch validation MAE from each, and average them into one curve.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 4.20 --- averaging MAE curves}{listings/ch04-27.py}
\begin{iband}[signal]
The averaged curve flattens around \textbf{epoch 120--140} and worsens after. \hilite{That is the stopping point}, and it is far more trustworthy than any single fold's curve.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 4.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The final model, and what its error means}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Train once more on all the training data, to the epoch the averaged curve identified, then evaluate on the test set.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{the production model}{listings/ch04-28.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch04-29.txt}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\istat{$\approx$ \$31,000}{average error, at the 100k scaling}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\istat{$\approx$ \$283,000}{what a prediction of 2.83 means}
\end{minipage}%
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Across all three examples}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Why every model here was kept small}
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.2068\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.188\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.2068\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3384\textwidth}}
\thead{Example} & \thead{Training samples} & \thead{Hidden layers} & \thead{Reasoning} \\ \midrule
IMDB & 15,000 & 2 $\times$ 16 units & Two classes, so 16 units is comfortably above the floor. \\
Reuters & 8,982 & 2 $\times$ 64 units & 46 classes: anything much narrower becomes a bottleneck. \\
Housing & 480 & 2 $\times$ 64 units & Tiny dataset --- a larger model would memorise it outright. \\
\end{itable}
\begin{iband}[signal]
The rule pulls in two directions at once: \textbf{wide enough not to bottleneck the classes, small enough not to memorise the samples}. Chapter 5 turns that tension into a method.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Across all three examples}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Four ways these workflows go wrong}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardbad}
\cardh{Training to a fixed epoch count}
Picking 20 epochs because a tutorial did. The turning point is a property of \textbf{your} data and has to be measured.
\end{icardbad}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardbad}
\cardh{Reusing a trained model across folds}
\inlinecode{get\_model()} must be called \textbf{inside} the K-fold loop. Reusing one carries knowledge between folds and voids the score.
\end{icardbad}
\end{minipage}%


\vskip 4pt

\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardbad}
\cardh{Normalising with test statistics}
An information leak, and it inflates your score in a way you will not discover until production.
\end{icardbad}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardbad}
\cardh{Reporting accuracy with no baseline}
80\% is excellent against 19\% and poor against 90\%. The number alone says nothing.
\end{icardbad}
\end{minipage}%
\end{frame}
\note{Every one of these shows up in the group assignments. Naming them now saves a lot of rework later.}

\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The table you will keep coming back to}

\thead{Task} & \thead{Last-layer activation} & \thead{Loss function} & \thead{Typical metrics} \\ \midrule

\textbf{Multilabel} & \inlinecode{sigmoid} (N units) & \inlinecode{binary\_crossentropy} & accuracy, ROC AUC \\

\end{itable}

\framekicker{Summary}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{What has to survive this chapter}
\begin{isteps}
\item \textbf{Vectorise} discrete data; \textbf{normalise features using training-set statistics only}.
\item \textbf{Intermediate layers must not be narrower than the class count} --- otherwise you build an information bottleneck.
\item \textbf{Little data $\rightarrow$ a small model}, one or two hidden layers.
\item \textbf{Train until it overfits to find the turning point}, then retrain to exactly that epoch.
\item \textbf{Little data $\rightarrow$ K-fold}, not a single validation split --- and read the spread, not just the mean.
\item Always compare against a \textbf{common-sense baseline} before deciding a score is good.
\end{isteps}
